sections.markdown:
## C — Driving under the influence: alcohol and drug effects, marijuana limits, implied consent, illegal per se limits, administrative and criminal penalties, young drivers, open containers, impaired-driver clues, and license suspensions and revocations
Knowledge domain: how alcohol and drugs impair driving, the legal alcohol and marijuana limits in Nevada, what implied consent means, the administrative and criminal penalties for DUI by offense, the special rules for young drivers, the open container law, how to spot an impaired driver, and the situations that cost a Nevada driver the license.

FACT_ID: sec12-F01 | anchor: A01
Alcohol slows brain function, affects how you process information and delays hand-eye coordination, and driving above the .08 legal limit raises crash risk from 5 times to as much as 30 times. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec12-F02 | anchor: A01
Both medical drugs and illegal or prescription-controlled drugs can seriously harm motor skills and the ability to think and react, so do not drive under their influence. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec12-F03 | anchor: A01
Although marijuana is legal in Nevada, it is unlawful to drive or be in actual physical control of a vehicle with more than two nanograms of marijuana per milliliter of blood, or five nanograms of marijuana metabolite. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec12-F04 | anchor: A01
Nevada DUI law has two kinds of penalties: administrative action by the DMV, taken regardless of what the court finds, and criminal action by the courts. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec12-F05 | anchor: A01
Under the Implied Consent Law, a driver an officer suspects of DUI will be asked to take a blood, breath or urine test, and an officer may order a blood draw even on a first offense. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec12-F06 | anchor: A01
Refusing the officer-directed tests revokes your driving privilege, with no eligibility for 1 year on a first refusal or 3 years if your privilege was revoked for refusal in the prior 7 years (NRS 484C.220). [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec12-F07 | anchor: A01
Under the Illegal Per Se Law, a chemical test showing .08% alcohol concentration or more, or any detectable amount of a controlled substance, revokes your driving privilege. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec12-F08 | anchor: A01
A driver under 21 whose test shows an alcohol concentration of .02% or more but under .08% loses the driving privilege administratively, and the officer can take the license on the spot. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec12-F09 | anchor: A01
The .08% level is only a guide, and you can be arrested and convicted of DUI at a lower alcohol concentration. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec12-F10 | anchor: A01
Whenever you lose your license, you can request an administrative hearing through the DMV. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec12-F11 | anchor: A02
An administrative illegal per se action for .08% or a detectable controlled substance revokes the driver license for 185 days, may require an SR-22, and may be followed by criminal penalties. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F12 | anchor: A02
For a commercial driver license holder, the administrative per se level starts at .04% alcohol concentration. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F13 | anchor: A02
On the penalty page, drivers under 21 at .02% alcohol concentration also have the license revoked for 185 days, may need an SR-22, and may face criminal penalties. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F14 | anchor: A02
A first DUI conviction brings license revocation for at least 185 days, two days to six months in jail or 48 to 96 hours of community service, and a fine of $400 to $1,000. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F15 | anchor: A02
A first DUI offender also pays DUI school tuition, averaging about $150, and may be ordered into treatment when the blood or breath alcohol was .08% or more. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F16 | anchor: A02
A second DUI within 7 years brings a one-year revocation, 10 days to 6 months in jail or residential confinement, a $750 to $1,000 fine and 100 to 200 hours of community service. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F17 | anchor: A02
A third or later DUI within 7 years brings a three-year revocation, 1 to 6 years in prison and a $2,000 to $5,000 fine, plus possible registration suspension and at least 3 years of treatment if ordered. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F18 | anchor: A02
A DUI that causes death or serious injury brings a three-year revocation, 2 to 20 years in prison and a fine of $2,000 to $5,000. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F19 | anchor: A02
A DUI offender's driving privilege can be reinstated immediately if issued a license with an ignition interlock restriction and an interlock device is installed, at the driver's own expense, in every vehicle they drive. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F20 | anchor: A03
A licensed driver under 18 whom juvenile court finds drove under the influence of alcohol or a controlled substance loses the license for 185 days. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F21 | anchor: A03
Drivers under 18 found to have driven under the influence by juvenile court, and drivers under 21 convicted of DUI, must undergo an alcohol or drug abuse evaluation, and the judge may order treatment. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F22 | anchor: A03
Nevada's open container law bans opened alcoholic beverages in the driver and passenger areas of a moving vehicle, except in motor home or house trailer living quarters and the passenger areas of commercial buses, limousines and taxis. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F23 | anchor: A03
Having passengers under 15 in the vehicle during a DUI is treated by the court as an aggravating factor in sentencing. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F24 | anchor: A03
A DUI conviction or guilty plea where a chemical test was done adds a $60 fine to cover the cost of the analysis. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F25 | anchor: A03
Clues of an impaired driver include turning too widely, straddling the center line or lane markers, weaving or drifting, nearly hitting things, and driving into oncoming traffic. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F26 | anchor: A03
More impairment clues: driving far too slowly, stopping in traffic for no reason, erratic or jerky braking, slow responses to signals, sudden speed changes, abrupt or illegal turns, and driving at night with headlights off. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F27 | anchor: A03
You can report a suspected drunk driver or any highway emergency from a cell phone anywhere in Nevada by dialing *NHP (*647). [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F28 | anchor: A04
A suspended or revoked license is never reinstated automatically; you must reapply at a DMV office, present name, birth date and Social Security documents, meet any other requirements and pay reinstatement fees. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F29 | anchor: A04
A license can be suspended or revoked for 12 or more demerit points in 12 months, for DUI by test result or conviction, and for causing a collision with a pedestrian or bicyclist. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F30 | anchor: A04
Failing to appear in court as required after a traffic ticket can cost you your license. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F31 | anchor: A04
If you have no liability insurance and a crash causes more than $750 in personal injury or property damage, both your driver license and your vehicle registration are suspended. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F32 | anchor: A04
Failure to maintain insurance leads to suspension when a required proof of financial responsibility is not provided, after a conviction for no insurance, or after repeated coverage lapses. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F33 | anchor: A04
Owing overdue court-ordered child support, a graffiti conviction, and organizing or joining street racing or trick-driving displays can each cost a person the license. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F34 | anchor: A04
Juveniles can lose the license for certain firearms offenses and for buying, drinking or possessing alcohol or using, possessing, selling or distributing controlled substances. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0082]

Misconceptions: staying under the per se alcohol limit does not make you legal if you are impaired; refusing a test does not avoid a penalty, it brings revocation; legal marijuana is not legal to drive on above the blood limit; an administrative revocation happens regardless of the court case; a suspended license does not come back by itself; the open container law covers passengers too, not just the driver.
Mnemonics: point oh eight for adults, point oh two under twenty-one, point oh four for commercial; a hundred eighty-five days, then one year, then three years of revocation for first, second and later DUI convictions; star N H P to report.
Glossary: DUI means driving under the influence; implied consent means agreeing to chemical testing by driving in Nevada; illegal per se means a test level that is a violation by itself; administrative penalty means action by the DMV; criminal penalty means action by a court; ignition interlock means a breath-testing device that must be passed before the engine starts; open container means an opened alcoholic beverage in the vehicle.
Dynamic facts: DUI fines, jail ranges, the DUI school cost estimate and the reinstatement fees are set by statute or vary over time, so confirm them with the Nevada DMV.
